role.title: Controls / Automation Engineer (Security Duties)
role.description: DRAFT. Designs, programs, commissions and maintains control systems (PLCs, HMIs, drives, and the networks that connect them) and is responsible for the security of the logic and configurations they own. NICE has no role for the engineers who write and change controller programs; NICE work role DD-WRL-009 covers OT security engineering but not control system programming.
role.overlaps_method: Computed: NICE roles sharing the most statements with this role, excluding the roles it extends.

citations.locator: §3.3.2 Build and Train a Cross-Functional Team (PDF p. 55)
citations.note: Names control engineers as members of the OT cybersecurity team.
Secure coding practices aimed at the engineers who program PLCs.

open_questions: Is one role right for both design-side controls engineers and plant-floor automation technicians, or should they be split?
Should this role inherit any of DD-WRL-009, or stay standalone with selected statements as now?

statements.text: Maintain backups of controller programs, configurations and firmware, verify their integrity, and test restoration

citations.note: Back up PLC logic and configuration; verify backups for reliability and integrity; test restoration. Firmware is a nice-plus addition.

statements.text: Establish a process to detect unauthorized changes to controller logic, parameters and setpoints by comparing running programs against approved baselines

citations.note: Hashes can validate the integrity of program logic.

citations.locator: Appendix C.3 Threat Events and Incidents (PDF p. 196)
citations.note: Manipulation of control: unauthorized changes to programmed instructions.
System integrity requirements.

statements.text: Define controls for transient cyber assets and removable media brought into production areas

citations.note: Restricts removable media and devices on OT nodes; does not use the term transient cyber assets.

statements.text: Schedule cybersecurity changes (e.g., patches, firmware updates, firewall rule changes) around production schedules and planned downtime, with tested rollback

citations.note: Schedule changes in maintenance downtime to limit impact.
Test patches in a test environment first.

statements.text: Assess the security of engineering workstations and controller programming software

citations.note: RBAC on engineering workstations.

statements.text: Apply secure coding practices to controller programs (e.g., validate HMI inputs and timer values in the controller, check physical plausibility, add integrity checks)

citations.note: Integrity checks; validate timers and counters; validate HMI inputs at the PLC; validate inputs by physical plausibility.

statements.text: Disable unneeded services, ports and default accounts on controllers, HMIs and network devices during commissioning

citations.note: Disable functions and services not required, with care for unintended impacts.
Disable unneeded communication ports and protocols.

statements.text: Identify the critical functions where cyber manipulation could cause unacceptable consequences, and focus security design effort on them first
Specify engineered controls early in design that eliminate or limit high-consequence cyber-enabled outcomes, instead of relying only on added IT security controls
Limit digital functionality to what each function needs, removing high-consequence, low-value complexity and latent capabilities that attackers could misuse
Evaluate, with safety, quality, maintenance and other disciplines, how misuse of a digital system could affect their areas of operation
Knowledge of industrial protocol families common in manufacturing (e.g., EtherNet/IP and CIP, PROFINET, Modbus TCP, OPC UA) and which security features each does or does not provide

citations.note: Discusses OT protocols and their security limitations; exact section not yet pinned.
Command messages sent over industrial protocols without authentication.

statements.text: Knowledge of controller programs and engineering project files (e.g., IEC 61131-3 ladder diagram, structured text, function block diagram) as security-critical assets

statements.text: Knowledge of how cyber events in manufacturing become production consequences such as line stoppage, scrap, latent quality defects and equipment damage

modules.objective: Identify unauthorized setpoint modifications in Structured Text.
Execute recovery steps and verify logic integrity after a controller reflash.
Analyze ladder logic to detect unauthorized changes.
Detect unauthorized logic changes in Structured Text.
Interpret control logic and correlate behavior to a physical process.
Compare baseline vs modified logic state for hidden manipulation.
Identify a hidden logic override in a ladder logic comparison.
